title: Reverse vs. Total Shoulder Replacement: Which One, and What Recovery Looks Like
seo_title: Reverse vs. Total Shoulder Replacement: Which Fits?
description: Why the rotator cuff decides between a reverse and a standard total shoulder replacement, who each one is for, and what recovery and pain look like.
body_html:
If shoulder arthritis or a badly torn rotator cuff has reached the point where replacement is on the table, you will hear two terms: total shoulder replacement and reverse shoulder replacement. They treat different shoulders, and the deciding factor is not the arthritis itself. It is the state of your rotator cuff. Here is how the two compare, how to tell which one fits, and what recovery looks like for each.

What is the difference between a reverse and a total shoulder replacement?

The shoulder is a ball and socket. The ball sits at the top of the upper arm bone, the socket is a shallow cup on the shoulder blade, and the rotator cuff (four muscles and their tendons) keeps the ball centered while the arm moves.

A standard total shoulder replacement copies that arrangement. The worn ball and socket surfaces are replaced with smooth implants in the same positions, so the shoulder still relies on a working rotator cuff.

A reverse shoulder replacement swaps the parts. The ball is fixed to the socket side, and a cup goes on top of the arm bone. That change in mechanics lets the deltoid, the large muscle over the outside of the shoulder, lift the arm without help from the rotator cuff.

Total (standard) shoulder replacementReverse shoulder replacement
DesignBall and socket in their natural positionsBall and socket swapped
What lifts the armThe rotator cuff and deltoid, as in a normal shoulderMainly the deltoid
Rotator cuff needed?Yes, intact and workingNo
Typical reasonArthritis in a shoulder with a healthy cuffA cuff torn beyond repair, often with arthritis that followed the tear

Why does the rotator cuff decide which one you get?

Because a standard replacement only works as well as the cuff holding it. If the cuff is intact and working, a standard total shoulder replacement is usually the better choice. If the cuff is torn beyond repair or no longer working, a standard replacement loses the muscle it depends on, and a reverse replacement is designed for exactly that shoulder.

So the question to ask is not “which is better?” but “what is my rotator cuff doing?” Neither design is an upgrade on the other. Each one is the right operation for a different problem.

Who is a total shoulder replacement for?

A standard replacement is usually considered when the joint surfaces are worn but the rotator cuff still works. Common reasons include:

  • Shoulder osteoarthritis, with stiffness and pain from worn cartilage
  • Rheumatoid or other inflammatory arthritis
  • Arthritis that developed after an old injury or fracture
  • Grinding or catching in the joint, night pain, and loss of strength reaching overhead

It is typically recommended once chronic pain is interfering with sleep, lifting or reaching, and therapy, injections or medication no longer give lasting relief.

Who is a reverse shoulder replacement for?

A reverse replacement is designed for a shoulder whose rotator cuff can no longer do its job, such as:

  • Rotator cuff tear arthropathy: arthritis that develops after a large, long-standing cuff tear lets the ball ride up out of position
  • A rotator cuff tear that can no longer be repaired, where the torn tendon has pulled back too far to reattach
  • Arthritis in a shoulder whose cuff is too weak or torn for a standard replacement to work well
  • Pain, night pain and an arm that will not lift, after therapy and other treatment have run their course

Is there anything to try before a shoulder replacement?

Usually, yes. A replacement is not the first answer for a torn rotator cuff. Tendinopathy and many partial-thickness tears settle with physical therapy and changes to how the shoulder is loaded, and for full-thickness tears in active people, surgical repair of the tendon is often considered. Rotator cuff tear treatment and repair covers those options, including arthroscopic repair, PRP and radial shockwave therapy for long-standing rotator cuff tendinopathy.

One point is worth knowing early. A tear caused by a specific injury, such as a fall or a heavy lift followed by sudden weakness, is worth having assessed promptly, because a torn tendon left alone can pull back and become harder to repair. Replacement is for shoulders where repair is no longer possible or has not worked.

What is recovery like after a reverse shoulder replacement?

The arm is protected in a sling for the first weeks. Therapy then brings back movement first and strength after, over several months. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS), you should be able to eat, dress and groom yourself within a few days, and some patients go home the same day while others stay one night.

The AAOS also lists precautions for the first six weeks, unless your surgeon gives you different ones:

  • Avoid extreme arm positions, such as reaching behind your body or holding the arm straight out to the side
  • Do not lift anything heavier than about 5 pounds, or the weight your surgeon recommends
  • Do not push yourself up out of a chair or bed with the operated arm
  • Do follow the home exercise program, and do not overdo it

Some long-term limits on heavy lifting may apply after a reverse replacement. Dr. Matarazzo goes through any that apply to your shoulder before surgery, so you know what to expect.

How long does pain last after reverse shoulder replacement?

It varies from person to person, so no honest answer comes with a fixed number of days. Some pain after surgery is a normal part of healing, and it is managed with a combination of medicines and a recovery plan built for you. The AAOS advises using opioids only as directed, for as short a time as possible, and talking to your doctor if your pain has not begun to improve within a few weeks.

Relieving the shoulder’s long-standing pain, including the night pain that often leads people to surgery, is one of the main reasons for the operation. If pain is getting worse instead of better, or comes with fever, redness or drainage from the wound, call the office.

How long is recovery after a total shoulder replacement?

The pattern is similar. Most patients regain daily use of the arm within weeks, with full strengthening over several months. Physical therapy is an essential part of it, restoring strength, flexibility and range of motion while supporting a safe return to daily activities. Once healed, low-impact and controlled strengthening activities are typically encouraged.

Will I be able to lift my arm again?

For a reverse replacement, restoring the ability to raise the arm, which a torn rotator cuff often takes away, is the main aim. How far it comes back depends on the shoulder, and expectations are set with you before surgery. After a standard total shoulder replacement, most patients see major improvement, especially in lifting and overhead reach, supported by rehabilitation.

How do you find out which one you need?

It takes an exam and imaging. Dr. Matarazzo tests the strength of the rotator cuff in each direction, then reviews X-rays and an MRI or CT scan to see the joint and the state of the cuff. Repair or non-surgical care comes first wherever it can still work. If replacement is the answer, you get a plain explanation of whether a reverse or standard design fits, and why.

If you have already been told you need a shoulder replacement and want another look before you decide, a second opinion is routine. Coverage depends on your plan; once a treatment plan is set, our staff verify your benefits with your carrier and walk you through what is covered before you commit.
